Speaker: D:
Text: Hi I’m Kendriana Drayton with the Oral History Program at the University of Florida.

Speaker: D:
Text: I’m here with Mr. John Bonaparte, I’m going to go ahead and allow him to introduce himself.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, and where were you born?

Speaker: B:
Text: I was born in South Carolina, .

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you born by a midwife or a hospital?

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, when you were growing up, did you have any family members in the military?

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you know what branches they served in?

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember when you first heard about the war?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t think I would make it.

Speaker: D:
Text: Would make it t o the war or from?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t think I’d get to the war.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, you thought I’d be over, hopefully?

Speaker: D:
Text: And so you said you were drafted —

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, did they give you much notice?

Speaker: D:
Text: Time to pack and get ready?

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, where did you have to report to?

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, about how long was your training?

Speaker: D:
Text: Alright, and in that training did you learn how to operate a gun?

Speaker: B:
Text: They were getting you ready to be enlisted into the Navy.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so you selected the Navy?

Speaker: B:
Text: I wanted the Army but they told me the Navy needed me, so I joined the Navy.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you had to go where you were needed?

Speaker: D:
Text: So, what was your impression of the Navy?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it what you thought it would be?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t want to be on the ground with the Army, so I chose the Navy.

Speaker: B:
Text: My first trip was Reykjavik, Iceland.

Speaker: D:
Text: When did you learn you were going to Iceland?

Speaker: B:
Text: I didn’t know until we got there.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you have to fight there?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, we was on a supply ship.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you get to interact with any of the locals?

Speaker: D:
Text: So your job in Iceland was to prep things?

Speaker: B:
Text: We carried food from different countries.

Speaker: B:
Text: We’d load up in New York or New Jersey, then we’d take a trip to a foreign country.

Speaker: B:
Text: So my first ship went to Iceland.

Speaker: B:
Text: The second ship we was in Newfoundland on retention.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then we took a trip about every month.

Speaker: B:
Text: So we’d go to Guantanamo Bay, and we was in Havana, different islands —Puerto Rico.

Speaker: D:
Text: Was it different in those different islands?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was the interactions there different than when you got back to the U S?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, the islands were mostly tourists.

Speaker: B:
Text: Most of them were tourist islands but they had bases on them, bases on the islands.

Speaker: D:
Text: While you were traveling and serving in the service, did you keep in close touch with your family?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, when we came in, we came in through the port.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you can afford it you could go home because it took about fifteen days to load up.

Speaker: D:
Text: So how would you contact your family?

Speaker: B:
Text: I usually took the train and would come home.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you serve along with different races of people?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, we had a White crew across from our compartment.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you want to tell me more about that?

Speaker: B:
Text: We were just like one big, happy family.

Speaker: D:
Text: So what was a typical day like on the ship?

Speaker: B:
Text: On a typical day we had movies, we had plenty of food because we hauled food.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of food did you eat?

Speaker: B:
Text: We carried all types of food.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, did you cook any of the food?

Speaker: D:
Text: So what were some of your duties besides transporting the food?

Speaker: B:
Text: Our duties — we had regular battle station practice for if we had any action, we had battle stations.

Speaker: B:
Text: Y eah, drills to operate guns, and aircraft guns.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you all have to use separate equipment?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was there segregation within the units?

Speaker: D:
Text: So was there any difference from home?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, you were closer to different people when you were on the ship.

Speaker: B:
Text: At home, you could separate yourself.

Speaker: B:
Text: So we had to be around different people.

Speaker: B:
Text: But this was a time when they had White and Black faucets and places where Whites and Blacks couldn’t go.

Speaker: B:
Text: That was home and aboard ship, too.

Speaker: B:
Text: Would they remind you of it?

Speaker: B:
Text: Let’s see, you still would need to be corrected.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you’re saying when you would come home you could separate yourself?

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so can we rewind a little bit to maybe right before you enlisted?

Speaker: D:
Text: We’re going to go back a little bit, okay?

Speaker: D:
Text: So, did you go to high school?

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you get to school every day?

Speaker: D:
Text: To get there and to get back home?

Speaker: D:
Text: Who were your teachers, or did you have any favorite teachers?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I had a favorite teacher.

Speaker: B:
Text: My first -grade teacher, when I came out of the service I went to Saint Augustine.

Speaker: B:
Text: They put on a train, and my first- grade teacher was there trying to get her other two years.

Speaker: D:
Text: So she was still getting some school in too?

Speaker: B:
Text: She was there trying to get her four years.

Speaker: B:
Text: They allowed Black teachers to teach two years at that time.

Speaker: B:
Text: I was surprised to see my first- grade teacher , meeting her in college.

Speaker: D:
Text: So what college was in Saint Augustine?

Speaker: D:
Text: It was good to see her ?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I was surprised to see her.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, did you hope to go to college after school or were you thinking Army?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I had a feeling to go to college because my high school years I was a printer.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I learned to be a printer.

Speaker: B:
Text: When I worked as a printer, I was sent to this job by the government to work as a printer.

Speaker: B:
Text: After I worked with this White guy, he  came up to me—I worked with him five years.

Speaker: B:
Text: And this was under the government.

Speaker: B:
Text: When he got a job, he got a job at a big newspaper company in Palatka.

Speaker: B:
Text: He came up to me one day and said—I was out of a job—He didn’t want to trust me.

Speaker: B:
Text: I think I knew more than he did, but he got the job.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, after that you stopped working in printing?

Speaker: B:
Text: So, after that I  — he didn’t know I was a carpenter.

Speaker: B:
Text: So I went into the building trade.

Speaker: B:
Text: I worked the company for twenty years —

Speaker: B:
Text: I worked for myself for about ten years, until I retired.

Speaker: D:
Text: And where did you do most of your work?

Speaker: D:
Text: So, you talk about your uncles serving in the service, in the Army.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were any members of your family part of the Masons or any other organizations?

Speaker: D:
Text: So did you vote before you enlisted?

Speaker: D:
Text: Or when did you first vote?

Speaker: B:
Text: After I came back from the service.

Speaker: D:
Text: And that was around what time?

Speaker: D:
Text: What was the community like when you came back home?

Speaker: B:
Text: The community was actually the same, little improvement.

Speaker: D:
Text: Can you tell us about your voting experience?

Speaker: D:
Text: Was there any hardships in going to do it?

Speaker: B:
Text: I have my choices when I do vote.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever hear about your parents talking about voting?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did they talk about what it meant to them?

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of changes have you seen since you’ve been here?

Speaker: D:
Text: Right, you came back to Crescent City?

Speaker: D:
Text: You said you were born in South Carolina; do you know if you had any ancestors or family members that served in the government?

Speaker: D:
Text: As far as like politicians, or?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you hear your parents or grandparents talk about slavery?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yes, my grandmother used to talk about it.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, what kind of changes did you notice during desegregation, which would be about the 70s?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, it’s been a change, but it needs to be better, you know?

Speaker: D:
Text: You said it a few times, it hasn’t changed much,.

Speaker: B:
Text: It seems like we’re going backwards now.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you feel like family is still really important?

Speaker: D:
Text: So let’s go back to Florida Nor mal.

Speaker: D:
Text: How did you get to college every day, or how often did you go?

Speaker: B:
Text: We rented a house; I had a house.

Speaker: B:
Text: As I said, about a hundred a month.

Speaker: D:
Text: And you worked as a printer to pay the rent?

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so what was your college day like?

Speaker: B:
Text: We had classes and I worked at the—I did the college letterheads and all the papers they used.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you have any White professors or any White staff at the school?

Speaker: B:
Text: This school was a predominately Black college.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, so most of your teachers were Black?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, most of them were Black.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, what other kind of things did they have at the college?

Speaker: B:
Text: It was an agriculture college, too.

Speaker: B:
Text: They raised different types of stocks, cows and sheep, goats, ducks.

Speaker: B:
Text: More or less, and industrial college.

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, the government, you know —It was close, I think.

Speaker: B:
Text: And they had that particular trade, too.

Speaker: B:
Text: I could’ve gone to Daytona or some place like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: You didn’t think about trying to integrate a White college?

Speaker: B:
Text: It wouldn’t have made any difference because I just met the wrong man when I was in my profession.

Speaker: B:
Text: I worked with the wrong person.

Speaker: D:
Text: well I think we got pretty good details so just to kind of wrap this up, were there any other times that you served in the military?

Speaker: D:
Text: And the highest rank you said you were?

Speaker: D:
Text: First- class a nd you did sustain any injuries during your service?

Speaker: D:
Text: Is there anything else you would like to add?

Speaker: B:
Text: I was in the VFW  for thirty -five years.

Speaker: D:
Text: What kind of things did you all do when you first started?

Speaker: B:
Text: D ifferent —What it is —VFW is an organization for the veterans, and what they do, they give out scholarships and stuff like that.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, did you all have a meeting place?

Speaker: D:
Text: This was a building or a lodge somewhere around Crescent City?

Speaker: B:
Text: I was actually joined by one of the mi ddlists back in 1975.

Speaker: D:
Text: Over the years have there been more Black soldiers to join?

Speaker: B:
Text: Mmhm, we had quite a few Blacks in there.

Speaker: B:
Text: And I was in the Lion Club for six years.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you got a part of different community organizations?

Speaker: B:
Text: Because it helps people in the community.

Speaker: B:
Text: And I was on the trades at the high school.

Speaker: D:
Text: At your high school, at Stanton?

Speaker: B:
Text: yeah there was a trade department.

Speaker: B:
Text: I was on there for seventeen years at my high school.

Speaker: D:
Text: So did you go and do work there or did you just —?

Speaker: B:
Text: We would go over there with the kids that took different trades and all that — mechanics and builders.

Speaker: D:
Text: So did you all teach them?

Speaker: D:
Text: So you worked as a teacher as well.

Speaker: B:
Text: What we’d do, we’d have meetings to keep it going.

Speaker: B:
Text: See, it was sponsored by the state.

Speaker: B:
Text: They stopped for some reason; they don’t have trades in the schools anymore, not in this county.

Speaker: B:
Text: They used to have different trades: mechanic, they had a building trade, they had welding, all through mechanics and stuff like that.

Speaker: B:
Text: But they don’t have it anymore, see?

Speaker: B:
Text: That’s the one thing they need to have in these schools now.

Speaker: B:
Text: They need to teach these women how to cook, they need that back in school!

Speaker: D:
Text: So we got some trades and homecare that needs to be taken care of?

Speaker: B:
Text: I’ve been in quite a few organizations.

Speaker: D:
Text: So, you’re still being active after you’re out of the service?

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever have any type of resistance from the White community?

Speaker: B:
Text: They all helped, anything we got into, they participated and helped us keep going.

Speaker: D:
Text: So how did you land in Crescent City?

Speaker: B:
Text: When I went to the service, my mother married a guy from this area.

Speaker: B:
Text: And when I came out, I moved down here.

Speaker: B:
Text: So I settled in Crescent City.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you know why they left South Carolina originally?

Speaker: D:
Text: So, Florida was a good opportunity?

Speaker: B:
Text: Most of my people moved from South Carolina to New York, all but my mother.

Speaker: B:
Text: And that’s where we were raised, up in Jacksonville.

Speaker: D:
Text: But you got to visit New York?

Speaker: B:
Text: Most of the time, I flew.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you have to stop at certain places during segregation or could you go?

Speaker: B:
Text: You know, for driving we had to stop at a motel one night.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, well in your two years of service did you have any reflections?

Speaker: D:
Text: Just did what you was told to do?

Speaker: B:
Text: I enjoyed the little time I was in there.

Speaker: D:
Text: You got to go a lot of places?

Speaker: D:
Text: And so after you were out, you didn’t choose to sign up again, right?

Speaker: B:
Text: By the time I got out on port, the war was over with, see?

Speaker: B:
Text: You had points, that’s why I didn’t stay in long.

Speaker: B:
Text: Other than that, I could’ve resigned, I could’ve went on and retired.

Speaker: D:
Text: Is there anything else you would like to add?

Speaker: B:
Text: I can say this, we supplied the convoy with food that was protecting the carrier that they signed a peace treaty on.

Speaker: B:
Text: Japanese signed the peace treaty, the carrier that was in the convoy of the ship out in the Atlantic?

Speaker: B:
Text: We served food to the ships that was protecting that carrier.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you served the ships that were protecting that treaty?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, we was on the ships that supplied the convoy.

Speaker: B:
Text: See, the convoy ships protected the carrier, so we supplied the ships that was protecting the carrier with food.

Speaker: D:
Text: How was that, working with the different classes of service, serving people?

Speaker: B:
Text: We got the chance to meet different kinds of people on different ships.

Speaker: B:
Text: Learned the name of a lot of ships.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you learn to speak any different languages?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, I never spoke any different language.

Speaker: B:
Text: I went to a lot of Spanish ports, but I never did speak any of their language.

Speaker: B:
Text: When I went to Iceland, Iceland—I don’t think there’s any Black people there.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you were the only ones?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, we were the only ones.

Speaker: B:
Text: They looked at us like you were something different, you know?

Speaker: B:
Text: Newfoundland, there were no Black people there.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, we’d go out to these different places and then we came back and started going to Bermuda, Trinidad, and then Cuba.

Speaker: D:
Text: And you said you stayed about a month in each place?

Speaker: B:
Text: It’d take longer to load up the ship than it did to unload the ship.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you remember how much you got paid?

Speaker: B:
Text: We never got over a hundred and fifty dollars a month.

Speaker: B:
Text: We were issued our suits and things.

Speaker: D:
Text: So you were pretty good, health- wise.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever have to go to the doctor when you were in enlisted?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, I was in good shape until I got older.

Speaker: D:
Text: Any other memorable things from where you’ve been, those different places?

Speaker: D:
Text: The different things about the different places?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, it’s —climate -wise, Iceland was a freezing place all the time.

Speaker: B:
Text: Puerto Rico and Trinidad, it was hot all the time.

Speaker: B:
Text: You had to be a swimmer.

Speaker: D:
Text: Do you still have any of your medals or awards at home?

Speaker: B:
Text: I wear them on my VFW cap.

Speaker: D:
Text: Okay, I’d like to get a picture of that.

Speaker: D:
Text: And then if you would like to share anything else, we can do this again, okay?

Speaker: B:
Text: Let me tell you everything on—

Speaker: D:
Text: All right, well, I’ll look to th at.

Speaker: D:
Text: All right, well, thank you Granddad.

Speaker: D:
Text: Where are you going to work?

Speaker: B:
Text: I got another thing, I wonder if he probably just kept them from me or something.

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I need to go over one day and just talk to them.

Speaker: B:
Text: Tell the guys over at the house eleven, he knows that piece is important.

Speaker: B:
Text: I have pictures of everywhere I went and everything I took.

Speaker: B:
Text: I took a picture sitting on the White House steps .

Speaker: D:
Text: You went to the White House?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, I was at the White House sitting on the White House steps !

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you go as a tourist or were you invited?

Speaker: B:
Text: You couldn’t get there now; you couldn’t do it.

Speaker: D:
Text: Were you invited by the president?

Speaker: B:
Text: No, I was in Washington, and I went to the White House and took a picture sitting on the steps.

Speaker: B:
Text: I wanted to save, because everybody would be disputing me if I said it.

Speaker: B:
Text: I took my train in Maryland, it isn’t far.

Speaker: B:
Text: You can travel over there in a little bit.

Speaker: B:
Text: No, that was in—Camp Blanding is where I went to be received.

Speaker: B:
Text: They sent me from there to Annapolis, Maryland.

Speaker: B:
Text: That’s where the Naval Academy is, I was there about a month.

Speaker: B:
Text: And then from there I got on a ship.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you have a bed or a cot?

Speaker: B:
Text: We slept in bunks, three- bed bunks.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you serve with some people from around here or were they all new people?

Speaker: B:
Text: I found one guy from Florida.

Speaker: B:
Text: I haven’t been able to find him yet, since I came out I been looking for him.

Speaker: B:
Text: Jim Ammons , he was supposed to be from down in Deland.

Speaker: D:
Text: So kind of close, Deland you said?

Speaker: B:
Text: Yeah, he was somewhere down around Deland .

Speaker: B:
Text: Lake Allen , that’s where he’s from, Lake Allen .

Speaker: D:
Text: So what do you do now to pass your time?

Speaker: D:
Text: What would you encourage young Black children to grow up to do?

Speaker: D:
Text: Go to school or look into the military or?

Speaker: B:
Text: The military is very good, they pay good money.

Speaker: B:
Text: If you stay long enough, you can get the education there.

Speaker: B:
Text: I advise most kids to find a school.

Speaker: D:
Text: What about doing things in the community?

Speaker: B:
Text: Well, you get into some organizations to help people in the community,

Speaker: B:
Text: You have these organizations, they have the Lions Club now, the VFW, they got one or two of those clubs uptown.

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you ever meet any civil rights figures?

Speaker: B:
Text: We had little clubs and things around here.

Speaker: B:
Text: We got this Boys to Men—

Speaker: D:
Text: Did you say where you were born in South Carolina?
